newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ASSEMBLY CAR PARK ROW COMES TO A HEAD.
newsitem.headline: EU ASSEMBLY CAR PARK ROW COMES TO A HEAD.

text.p: The European Parliament will refuse to take delivery of its costly new headquarters until a row over the new building's underground car park is resolved, parliament officials said on Tuesday.

The European Union assembly was due to move into the 40 million Belgian francs ($1.2 billion) building on April 1, but it has now decided to sit tight unless it is given the 2,300 parking spaces which developers Societe Forum Leopold (SEL) originally promised.
"There was a decision not to take over the building unless the conditions in the contract were met," parliament spokesman Stig Berglind told Reuters.
The parliament is expected on Tuesday formally to advise SEL and the local authorities of the decision.

SEL is contractually bound to provide the assembly with all 2,300 parking spaces. But the regional environment ministry has refused to authorise the plans. It says the parliament can only have 900 spaces and must put the remainder to other uses.

Brussels residents and the city's environment agency cite a report by the European Commission recommending curbs on the number of cars EU civil servants bring into the city's European quarter in a bid to ease daily traffic jams and cut pollution.
SEL director Jacques Bellemans said he hoped the regional government would this week overrule Brussels Environment Minister Didier Gosuin and let the original contract stand.
Gosuin's office declined to comment on the dispute until it received formal notification of the EU assembly's decision.
Last month Gosuin challenged the parliament to state clearly before the end of March, when it is due to sign a 27-year lease on the new building, whether it needed all 2,300 parking places.

Berglind told Reuters the assembly currently needed room for only 1,500 cars but had catered for nearly twice that number out of foresight, in line with EU plans to expand from 15 to 25 members early next century.
He predicted pollution and traffic chaos would be even worse than at present if civil servants had to vie with locals for the few curbsides around their offices where parking was legal.

The only dissenting voice among parliament's 626 deputies comes from the 28-member Green group, which thinks the assembly should abide by the wishes of local people to cut car use, in return for a reduction in the price of the new building.
"Creating parking spaces encourages more cars," Magda Alvoet, the Belgian co-president of the Green group argued.
Rather than contributing to the problem, the parliament should encourage the local authorities to solve the problem by improving public transport services," Alvoet said.
Berglind said the Brussels authorities had been warned in 1989 they must tackle traffic problems in the European quarter.
"It is not up to the parliament to decide the traffic flow," he said.
